newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE 100 falters on profit-taking in drugs.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE 100 falters on profit-taking in drugs.

text.p: ** UK's FTSE 100 ends weaker on profit-taking but closes
well off day's worst levels despite lower Dow.
** Dow down 12 pts at London close. Gilts end firm.
** Drug stocks hit by profit-taking. Banks led higher by
HSBC. British Steel up on buy-back. BT off on MCI woes.
Britain's FTSE 100 index was dragged modestly lower as profit-taking hit the drugs sector on Thursday, but the market ended well off the day's lows after faltering on the brink of the 5,000 hurdle.
The blue-chip index finished 15.2 points lower to 4,949.0. Losses in the pharmaceutical stocks alone took 24 points off the index but losers and gainers were almost evenly matched.
"Pharmaceuticals got slaughtered today yet we were only down 15 points, which is quite encouraging really," said Ian Williams, UK equity strategist at Panmure Gordon.

At the start, the FTSE had powered to a new all-time high of 4,993.0, stopping just seven points short of the psychologically important 5,000 barrier after futures turned lower and profit-takers cashed in on the FTSE's four percent rise this week.
"There has been no real change in sentiment," said Williams. "People were just taking a few profits and waiting for the next leg upwards."

After dropping to a session low of 4,935.5 the FTSE halved its losses on the expectation of a firmer opening in New York, where the Dow had shattered the 8,000 barrier the previous day. Hopes were raised after U.S. housing starts and weekly jobless claims data came in much as expected.
But the Dow opened lower and succumbed to its own bout of profit-taking although leading U.S. stocks were down just 12 points as London markets closed.

A stronger gilts market softened the blow for UK equities with long gilt futures closing up sharply on the day. Dealers said the dip in stock prices today was nothing more than a normal correction after three straight record-breaking sessions.
"It's a natural correction," one said. "The market needed to catch its breath but it will have another go at 5,000."
Second-line stocks rose for the fifth consecutive day. The Mid-250 was up 12.6 points at 4,500.1.

But HSBC later eased to close at 21.79 stg, up 28p on the day. Another record run in Hong Kong and a shortage of stock as institutions continued to build up their weight in the sector had lifted the shares, dealers said.

Elsewhere, shares in British Telecom fell 4-1/2p to 441p in active trade. BT, pressured by a profit warning last week from merger partner MCI, fell as prospects of renegotiating the deal appeared to fade.
Volume in BT was beaten only by British Steel which finished 10-1/4 up at 159-3/4 after the company launched a share buy-back programme.
Mid-250 stocks however were still only up one percent from the start of the year, compared with a 20 percent rise in the leading index.
Whilst drug shares led the sell-off today a renewed surge in HSBC Holdings Plc continued to buoy the banks.
Among domestic share features heavyweights SmithKline Beecham Plc fell 3.25 percent, Glaxo Wellcome fell 4.25 percent and Zeneca Group lost over five percent or 115p to 21.50 stg.
A further rise in HSBC softened the blow as it hit a record peak of 22.17 stg.
Brokers Cazenove & Co told Reuters they had been asked to buy up to 100 million shares at 155p on behalf of the company.

Meanwhile, a positive stance on the insurance sector by analysts at NatWest Securities lifted shares in Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Group Plc. The stock gained 16p to 487-1/2p whilst General Accident was up 42-1/2p to 949.
-- Elaine Hardcastle, London Newsroom +44 171 542 4027
